name: Misal Pav
cuisine: Maharashtrian (Mumbai-style misal; Kolhapuri and Puneri styles noted below)

ingredients.name: Groundnut oil (or any neutral cooking oil)

equipment: Bowl and a thin cotton cloth (or a sprouting box / a steel colander with a plate on top) for sprouting
Small kadai or saucepan for the usal, and a second small kadai or pot for the kat
Tawa or frying pan for warming the pav
Spatula, ladle, serving bowl, small plate for toppings
Chopping board and knife, measuring spoons
Pressure cooker is NOT needed: matki sprouts cook in 8–10 min in a covered pan

steps.title: Rinse the matki
steps.text: Put 30 g (2½ tbsp) dry matki in a bowl, rinse in 2–3 changes of water and pick out any stones.
steps.visualCue: The water runs clear; no grit or stones left.
steps.cameraCheck: The rinsed matki in the bowl
steps.videoShot: Water swirling over the tiny beans, then poured off.

steps.title: Soak
steps.text: Cover with 250 ml (1 cup) water and leave it.
steps.visualCue: The beans swell to about double and look plump and smooth.
steps.videoShot: Before-and-after of the bowl.

steps.title: Drain and wrap
steps.text: Drain fully. Tie the beans loosely in a damp cotton cloth (or put them in a covered steel box) and keep in a warm, dark place.
steps.tip: Sprinkle a little water on the cloth if it dries out, especially in hot weather.
steps.visualCue: No standing water; the cloth is damp, not dripping.
steps.videoShot: Tying the cloth bundle.

steps.title: Wait for sprouts
steps.text: Leave until tails appear.
steps.tip: Don't let the tails grow longer than about 1 cm; they turn bitter. A sour smell or slime means discard and start again.
steps.visualCue: Most beans have white tails 3–5 mm long. They smell fresh and earthy, not sour.
steps.cameraCheck: A spoonful of sprouts close up
steps.videoShot: Opening the cloth to show the sprouted beans.

steps.title: Rinse the sprouts
steps.text: Rinse once and drain. You should have about 80 g (heaped ½ cup).
steps.visualCue: Clean sprouts, no loose husks floating.
steps.videoShot: Water running over the sprouts.

steps.title: Heat the oil
steps.text: Put a small kadai on medium heat and add 1 tsp (5 ml) oil.
steps.visualCue: The oil shimmers.
steps.videoShot: Oil spreading in the kadai.

steps.title: Splutter the mustard
steps.text: Add ⅛ tsp mustard seeds.
steps.visualCue: The seeds pop and crackle.
steps.videoShot: Mustard seeds jumping in the oil.

steps.title: Add the sprouts
steps.text: Add the 80 g sprouts, a pinch of turmeric and 1 g salt (⅙ tsp). Stir for 1 minute, then add 60 ml (¼ cup) water, cover and cook on low-medium.
steps.tip: Matki goes mushy fast. Check at 7 minutes. The usal should be fairly dry; the kat brings the liquid. Tip it into a bowl and set aside.
steps.visualCue: The sprouts are soft when pressed between fingers but still whole, not mushy. The water has almost dried up.
steps.cameraCheck: A sprout pressed on a spoon
steps.videoShot: Lifting the lid to show the steaming, yellow-tinged sprouts.

steps.title: Roast the coconut
steps.text: In the second pan on low heat, dry-roast 1½ tbsp (8 g) grated dry coconut, stirring.
steps.tip: It burns quickly; take it off as soon as it is golden. Move it to a plate.
steps.visualCue: Light golden-brown with a toasty, nutty smell.
steps.cameraCheck: The roasted coconut in the pan
steps.videoShot: Coconut shreds turning golden as they are stirred.

steps.title: Roast the onion
steps.text: In the same pan, heat ½ tsp oil on medium. Add 40 g sliced onion, the 2 garlic cloves and ½-inch ginger, roughly chopped.
steps.tip: Well-browned onion gives the kat its depth and colour. Don't rush this.
steps.visualCue: The onion is deep golden-brown at the edges; garlic is lightly golden.
steps.videoShot: Onion slices browning and shrinking.

steps.title: Add the tomato
steps.text: Add 40 g chopped tomato and cook.
steps.visualCue: The tomato softens and turns mushy.
steps.videoShot: Pressing a tomato piece flat with the spatula.

steps.title: Cool
steps.text: Tip the onion-tomato mix onto the plate with the coconut and let it cool.
steps.visualCue: Warm, not hot, to the touch.
steps.videoShot: The colourful mix spread on the plate.

steps.title: Grind the paste
steps.text: Put it in a small mixer jar with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and grind.
steps.tip: If the jar won't catch, add 1 tbsp more water, or grind a double batch (see Quick facts).
steps.visualCue: A smooth, thick, brown-orange paste with no coconut flecks.
steps.videoShot: Opening the jar to show the smooth paste.

steps.title: Temper
steps.text: Heat 1½ tsp (7.5 ml) oil in the pan on medium. Add ⅛ tsp cumin, a pinch of hing and 5 curry leaves.
steps.visualCue: Cumin sizzles and darkens a shade; curry leaves crackle and turn crisp.
steps.videoShot: Curry leaves crackling.

steps.title: Add the ground spices
steps.text: Turn the heat to low. Add 1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder, 1 tsp goda masala, ½ tsp coriander powder and a pinch of turmeric. Stir.
steps.tip: Low heat only; chilli powder burns in seconds. Have the paste ready.
steps.visualCue: The oil turns red and smells fragrant. No burning smell.
steps.videoShot: The spices blooming in the oil.

steps.title: Fry the paste
steps.text: Add the ground paste and stir on medium heat.
steps.visualCue: The paste darkens, thickens, and oil starts to separate at the edges.
steps.cameraCheck: Oil at the edge of the paste
steps.videoShot: The paste bubbling as oil seeps out.

steps.title: Add water, jaggery and salt
steps.text: Pour in 200 ml water, add ½ tsp (3 g) grated jaggery and ¼ tsp (1.5 g) salt. Stir.
steps.visualCue: A thin, orange-red gravy.
steps.videoShot: Water pouring in and swirling.

steps.title: Simmer the kat
steps.text: Bring to a boil, then simmer uncovered on low-medium.
steps.tip: Taste and adjust salt now. If it gets too thick, add 2–3 tbsp hot water.
steps.visualCue: A thin, pourable gravy (thinner than dal) with a layer of red oil ("kat") floating on top. Tastes spicy with a hint of sweetness.
steps.cameraCheck: The red oil layer on the surface
steps.videoShot: The gravy bubbling with red oil pooling on top.

steps.title: Chop the toppings
steps.text: Finely chop 25 g onion (3 tbsp) and 1 tbsp coriander leaves. Cut a lemon wedge.
steps.visualCue: Small, even onion pieces; fresh green coriander.
steps.cameraCheck: The toppings on a small plate
steps.videoShot: The knife chopping onion.

steps.title: Warm the pav
steps.text: Slit 2 pav sideways (not all the way through). Warm on a tawa on medium (with ½ tsp butter, optional), pressing lightly.
steps.visualCue: Light golden patches and soft, warm inside.
steps.videoShot: Pav pressed on the tawa, then flipped.

steps.title: Fill the bowl with usal
steps.text: Reheat the usal for 30 sec if it has cooled, then put it in a serving bowl.
steps.visualCue: A small mound of yellowish sprouts.
steps.videoShot: Spooning the usal into the bowl.

steps.title: Pour the kat
steps.text: Ladle about 1 cup (200 ml) of hot kat over the usal, including the red oil on top.
steps.visualCue: The sprouts are just submerged in red gravy.
steps.cameraCheck: The bowl of usal and kat
steps.videoShot: Ladling the steaming kat.

steps.title: Top and serve
steps.text: Just before eating, add 25 g (¼ cup) farsan, the chopped onion and coriander, and squeeze over the lemon wedge. Serve with the 2 pav.
steps.tip: Add the farsan only at the table; it goes soggy within minutes. Serve extra kat on the side to pour as you eat, as Mumbai places do.
steps.visualCue: A red bowl with a crunchy yellow farsan layer, white onion and green coriander on top.
steps.videoShot: Farsan sprinkled on, lemon squeezed, a piece of pav dipped.

reasons: sprouted matki is a good base, giving plant protein and fibre (about 19 g protein and 12 g fibre in the full serving at home). The tomato-onion kat is mostly vegetables and spices. Points come off for the deep-fried farsan, white-flour pav and a high sodium load (about 1,500 mg). Restaurant versions float much more oil in the kat (the red "tari" layer is the selling point), add more farsan and often serve extra pav, which can push a plate well past 800 kcal (est.).

researchRating.basis: misal pav is one of Maharashtra's best-loved breakfasts, with dedicated misal-only restaurants across Mumbai, Thane and Pune and heavy coverage in food guides. Aaswad's misal (Dadar) won the Foodie Hub Global Awards "World's Tastiest Vegetarian Dish" in 2015. Recipe pages rate it very highly (Indian Healthy Recipes about 4.99/5 from 94 votes; Hebbar's Kitchen 5/5 from 187 votes on its Hindi page). Small deductions because it is too spicy for many diners, and reviews of famous spots often mention small portions for the price or uneven quality.

storage: Store the usal and kat separately, without toppings. Both keep in the fridge in airtight boxes for 2 days (refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking). The kat freezes well for up to 1 month; the usal can be frozen but the sprouts soften. Keep farsan and pav at room temperature in closed packs. To reheat: bring the kat to a full boil on the stove (add 2–3 tbsp water if thick) and warm the usal in a pan with a splash of water for 2 min, or microwave covered until steaming hot.
leftoverRemix: Misal bhel (matki chaat). Drain any leftover usal of gravy, chill it, and toss with chopped onion, tomato, cucumber, a squeeze of lemon, a pinch of chaat masala, 1 tsp green chutney and a handful of kurmura (puffed rice). Top with a little farsan. A cold, crunchy snack in 5 minutes. Leftover kat alone makes a quick "kat pav" or a spicy base for poha or a bowl of rice.
burnOff: about 9.8 km of running (685 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 13.7 km of brisk walking (about 2 h 45 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.). The misal bowl alone (about 500 kcal): about 7.1 km running or 10 km walking (est.).
